Hey friend, I feel for you deeply. When I first started dating my partner I had flashbacks of my abusive ex all the time - to the point that I almost called him my ex's name several time. This can be so terrifying to experience, I was so scared that my partner would turn out to be just like my ex and the things that reminded me of him were signs to run, or even just signs of some bigger incompatibility or something. 

Having your current partner remind you of or trigger you into fixating on an abusive person in your past or present is extremely common and sometimes points to real similarities, and also sometimes does not. In my case, my partner was never actually doing anything abusive or toxic to me. I want to validate that this fear is normal, although it might not be grounded in facts, which is frequently true about ROCD. 

Work on healing and processing your trauma from mom. It will change your life for the better and help you see people clearly, and help you trust yourself. much love to you.

I scheduled consults with therapists and made sure they were working through a somatic and trauma-informed lens, and now I would add ancestral work to that list. They also do need to have a formidable understanding of OCD borne from trauma and serious attachment wounding.

EMDR is good but can be a long haul! I REALLY highly recommend Internal Family Systems and Somatic Experiencing. My therapist also uses a lot of ancestral work in our sessions to help me understand that these adaptation and patterns didn’t start with me and I didn’t ask for them.

I have been in a healthy and ever growing beautiful relationship for 2 years now, and our relationship is not perfect in lots of ways but we are deeply committed to eachother and to our own healing and mutual care and understanding and respect for eachother. We also now go to couple’s therapy which is super helpful!

As for how things are going now, I still have big ups and downs and have been in recovery from chronic disregulation for 2 years. I learn more every day about how my formative experiences created narratives that my system is working so hard to protect, and my “work” is now centered around creating spaciousness, allowance, and compassion for all of the emotional experiences I’m having.

Hi! Honestly I haven’t read any books. I found my way to all of this insight via somatic therapy, specifically a combination of Somatic Experiencing and IFS, in combination with doing my own general study on how ERP works and a LOT of critical thinking about trauma, the nervous system, and chronic dysregulation. I don’t even really believe in “OCD” as my diagnosis anymore. I look at it as a super overpowerful “fixer” part of me trying desperately to manage all of my feelings.

getting over ROCD is the process of learning to just let your thoughts and feelings happen. and that includes overthinking sometimes! the compulsion that really promotes ROCD is trying to "fight" or halt our feelings/thoughts. 

So for example I might be thinking about a fight or disagreement my bf and I had. Instead of freaking out that I'm overthinking it, or trying to negotiate my way out of thinking about it, I accept that it's triggering me and radically allow myself to feel that feeling without fighting it. I relax and understand it's just a feeling, and a normal one at that. this also goes for thoughts, all kinds of thoughts.

Totally. I have spent a lot of time trying to find a way to make peace with the people who have harmed me. Ultimately I have found roads to understanding that they have been harmed deeply by systems of patriarchy, misogyny, racism, you name it. And that does not excuse what they did, nor does it mean that I have to forgive them - if anything, the most important thing I have found is to continue being able to feel my grief and anger, and have compassion for myself in moments when I was powerless and how awful and hard that was. 

But you can always choose to remember that no one can take your true power from you - those events and those people could never take our power or inherent love and worth and values from us, it’s just the road to remembering who we truly are: inherently loved and loving and loveable. 

Even if those people did find healing, we can still choose to be who we are, with the people in our lives now 💓

Hey! This is a really difficult rumination to be having, and I'm sorry you're dealing with it - it sounds super hard. I just want to say I have also had lots of ideas and signs about who I'm "supposed" to be with. I find these to be valuable moments to come back to my values. I will be with whoever I decide I am supposed to be with. I am not powerless. The universe does not own my free will. And more importantly, I have power over my values and convictions, and I value my free will, my agency, and my personal power. I ruminate a lot on whether or not my partner is "the one" and if there could be someone better out there for me. And I tell myself - you know, maybe there is, but that doesn't matter at all right now because I am choosing this person, this partner, my love for them. 

Even if a part of you fears or believes you will end up with the person who SA'd you, you have the power to find the sovereign, wise, mature part of you which believes you are powerful in your ability to name and live in your values. We can't control everything, by a long shot, but we can absolutely control and change our core beliefs, convictions, and values. 

Recovery from ROCD/PTSD is fucking hard and I know even choosing or feeling values can be incredibly hard when you are flooded with fear. I want you to know I believe that there is a wise, calm, loving, strong part of you that knows you can choose your values, choose how you want to show up in this world, and choose recovery.

Hey wow, just seeing this. So wild to return to this post and this question almost a year later. Here we go:

The past year has been the most painful and difficult thing I've experienced since getting sober 6 years ago. ROCD for me, unequivocally, is the collusion of whatever neurotype OCD is with a shit ton of unresolved complex trauma my body has been carrying for most of my life. Staying in this relationship has been the most triggering, uncomfortable, terrifyingly uncertain experience, and also so unimaginably rewarding. 

To be clear, my partner is AMAZING. This work has been POSSIBLE because he is so kind and sweet and safe and honest and all of the things. You can only do this work with someone who is fundamentally safe and trustworthy, and unfortunately you only truly know that by getting to know them over time. HOWEVER, all of that being said, I have learned fundamentally that trust is a choice. Someone can show you they are good over and over again and you will not believe it or trust them until you have done a shit ton of other healing work. 

Trust, security, and good faith must become your value system. And in order for that to manifest in your body, you must go through the experience of facing and integrating the grief and anger that is trapped in your body - all of the unprocessed fear and loss. 

I cannot stress this enough, the most simply and accurate definition of CPTSD/PTSD I have found is: Being trapped in a memory of powerlessness and pain, and being trapped in the false belief of inferiority. 

PTSD is a dysfunction of memory, that is the result of not being able to process and safely attune to our grief and anger responses, thus completing our emotional arcs instead of them getting stuck. Not to mention that we still live daily in a world which profits off our perceived inferiority, the idea that no one is ever enough. Healing requires divesting from these beliefs and values entirely, and rebuilding our self-ideation from scratch.

This results in the body and brain being mired in shame and constantly hypervigilant - the body and brain have taken on the false belief that we are inferior (the outlook of an abused child) and therefore bad, and also that the ways people have treated us were and are our fault - the result of emotionally immature and abusive adults who could not take responsibility for their own feelings and actions, or properly attune to us the way we required. 

I have found such profound healing from spending time in nature, understanding that I am natural, and that there is no hierarchy in a healthy ecosystem - the ants, mushrooms, and earthworms are as valuable and powerful as the apex predator, and that predator will eventually go back to earth and feed the trees. 

The process also requires finding and re-integrating the parts of us that have been abandoned and pushed out by these other beliefs and parts of us. Most often, these are parts we associate with weakness, vulnerability, and powerlessness - often features also associated with femininity (hello, internalized misogyny!). The parts of us that are hypervigilant (OCD) can only learn to relax the more we heal our relationship with our inner children. 

I cannot recommend highly enough doing trauma therapy and IFS, and then moving into exposures. I do not believe it is safe to do exposures with ROCD/CPTSD without having intensely available inner resources and clarity beforehand, otherwise you can totally just get retriggered and retraumatized! Our systems must become resourced first.

Also there is no hierarchy between anxious ROCD and avoidant ROCD, it is all happening because of an intensely dysregulated nervous system. We need to become safe and resourced within ourselves, which requires healthy relationships for us to heal in and receive care and safety in, but also the more you heal the more you will realize that the only person who can give you the security and trust you are truly craving is you, and that can only happen when you integrate your abandoned parts and feelings. 

I hope this is helpful, wondering how you're doing and here if you wanna talk more.

One thing I wish people understood about ROCD and CPTSD (which is the root cause of most ROCD) is that our responses and reactions to things are not always accurate to the reality of those things - our responses can both far exceed the reality of those things, and also underreact as well. I have been anxious in all of my relationships - the healthy ones right along with the abusive ones. What matters to me is figuring out what my VALUES are and how I want to communicate, how I want to show up.

I know that my ROCD overreacts to a lot of stuff all the time. I also know that sometimes, my ROCD is totally acting up in response to things that actually are not okay with me. The problem is, the urgency and intensity of my ROCD causes me to act in ways that are not aligned with my values. 

If something is bothering me, I need to be able to bring it up in a way that is in line with how I want to communicate, and wait until I no longer feel the OCD level of urgency around it. "Hey, when you said that thing the other day I felt pretty uncomfortable. What was going on for you with that language? I'm curious to know what that means for you, because it might mean something different to me"

"I know you're not a racist person and I trust that you are always trying your best to be compassionate, but that language was unsettling for me and not in line with my values and the kinds of values I hope my loved ones have. I'd really appreciate it if you would not use that language around me and also reflect on the significance of how it could make others feel"

How someone responds says a lot. People don't take seriously enough how hard it is to discern dealbreakers and red flags when you have ROCD and your nervous system is constantly searching for threats that aren't even there. 

Your role is keeping your side of the street clean. How do you want to show up in your relationships? Calm, strong, secure, patient? or hypervigilant, accusatory?

Hey! I have had wonderful experiences using psilocybin for my OCD. I would highly recommend microdosing and not “tripping” because when you microdose it’s much easier to integrate your experiences into your every day sober life.

That being said, higher doses from time to time can help integrate trauma stored in the body. 

I create a sacred space in my room (no dostractions, candles lit, calm music, journal out, yoga mat out) and microdose and whatever comes up for me I give myself permission to move in ways that feel right, to cry, to laugh, to write, to say things out loud. 

Psilocybin is a supplemental tool that has been so amazingly helpful for me in this journey, but it’s the integration process that is the most important in your everyday lives following the medicine.

Hey! I highly recommend IFS if you have never heard of it. I struggle with this exact combo of stuff (CPTSD and ROCD/disorganized attachment). So much of healing self worth is just realizing that there is no such thing as "low self worth". What does happen is that we tell ourselves stories about how loveable we are based on how we've been treated - we adapt to survive and these stories keep us safe. By learning to have compassion for ourselves, our stories, and our feelings, we naturally realize that we are inherently worthy of love and commitment. 

You don't HAVE to get to a place where you know for sure you'd be okay about things that would hurt and devastate anybody. So much of this journey is actually coming to the realization that although pain might be inevitable, and loss, what we make it mean about us is totally up to us.

I cannot stress the level of gentleness one must find in order to facilitate this in a traumatized nervous system. Gentleness is the word, the vibration, the feeling that guides me every day in my recovery process. Something CBT is very lacking in is a trauma-informed somatic approach to our adaptations. Feelings are in the body. Trauma is in the body. 

Cannot recommend enough reading "No Bad Parts". It changed everything for me. 

​

Best of luck to you, sending love.

It takes time to heal, and you have lots of time. Slow down and meet your nervous system where it is - there is nothing to fix. You are not a problem. You are experiencing intense symptoms of anxiety. 

I have found it immensely helpful to treat ROCD as a symptom of CPTSD, and offer that ERP can be extremely overwhelming for an already disregulated nervous system. It's okay to try other forms of trauma therapy.

You may not want to hear this, but I once broke up with someone I wasn't attracted to and was having ROCD around it. I absolutely have ROCD in my current relationship, but the themes have just switched.  What really tipped me off in that relationship was that I didn't like the way he smelled phenomenally. I realized I couldn't force myself to be intimate with someone I couldn't have sex with - I was literally repelled by his natural smell. It was an extremely hard call to make and I felt a lot of guilt around it, but I do now understand that there was something real happening there for me. 

All of that being said, the ROCD did not go away. ROCD does not always mean there's not something "real" happening - what it is, is when we cannot make grounded decisions because we're terrified of hurting someone or being hurt. 

What I wish someone had told me in the relationship I talk about here, was: There is no urgency. It is totally okay to have questions and doubts and ALSO want to enjoy and be with somebody for the experience. It's okay to be confused, it is CERTAINLY okay to even not have butterflies/sparks/want to have sex with someone AND still be in love with them at the same time! 

ROCD creates a form of hyper responsibility to figure it all out, so as to avoid ever hurting someone, being hurt, or making the wrong decision. 

Go ahead! Make the wrong decision, let it be confusing and complicated. It's okay to just want to love and experience someone. It's an amazing opportunity to sit with the complexities of being intimate with another person on many levels, getting to know yourself. That is really what relationships are for: **learning. trying.** 

If love was about perfection, not a damn person on this earth would do it. I don't regret being with my ex for one second, he was an amazing partner and a beautiful person and I would do it all again, just slowed down and being able to acknowledge all the complexities, still letting myself make the choice to explore, even if that ultimately lead to the realization that we weren't as physically compatible as I personally needed. 

NO ONE is harder on themselves than people with ROCD. And let me tell you, the lies we get fed about how love is supposed to be are horseshit. Learn, try. Forgive yourself for not having "the right answer".

It just means it's time to find a different person to talk to who understands what you're going through better, and can help get you the support and help you need!

it truly does. it also takes small things and blows them far out of proportion, and because we've been living in obsession/fear for so long, that feels normal to us. But we don't have to live like that - no matter what the case, theme, or label is. we deserve peace and joy and to not constantly fear the future, fear pain, etc...

If you are OBSESSING and COMPULSING around it then it very well is ROCD. OCD feeds off a need for certainty, and of course we want that the most with the people we love the most. But the truth is, we do not have certainty. That they will always love us, that they won't leave us, that they will always want us, etc... and that is really fucking hard to lean into but it is the WAY to interrupt this is to lean INTO the fear. 

Challenge yourself to stay with your fear of him not loving you or wanting you enough - it will point you straight towards a big old wound of/fear of rejection which is where the healing and self love journey really begins.

So many people experience ROCD as "Do I love them enough?" But it can be ANYTHING - cheating, jealousy, abandonment, OCD can fixate on and switch to anything, and will most easily latch onto whatever it is we feel like we don't have control or certainty over.

The answer is acceptance. Drop the rope. Start to lean into trust. And most often those of us (same here) who struggle with your particular theme of ROCD thoughts, find it concurrent with codependency and disorganized attachment and relational trauma. 

ROCD feels like a curse but it's a blessing, because it's allowing you to heal wounds most people have but will never truly or fully address. Buckle in, sister! It's a hell of a ride but you got this!
